headline.headline: BUCS BURY BREWERS, 14-5, IN PITTSBURGH SLUGFEST
headline.deck: Pirates erupt for 10 runs in the fourth inning to run Milwaukee off PNC Park
headline.body:
PITTSBURGH — The Pittsburgh Pirates turned PNC Park into a shooting gallery Sunday afternoon, pounding the Milwaukee Brewers 14-5 before 34,087 fans in a game that was effectively over by the time the fourth inning ended. The Pirates sent at least 10 runners across the plate in that one catastrophic frame for Milwaukee, turning a scoreless contest into a rout that starter Cody Gasser and his bullpen could not survive.

Winner Yoho, who also hit Bryan Reynolds twice with pitches, was on the mound long enough to collect the victory, while the Brewers cycled through relievers including Koenig and Gasser as Pittsburgh's lineup refused to stop swinging. Ryan O'Hearn was hit by a pitch from Gasser, adding to Milwaukee's miseries in a game where the Brewers managed only their lone three-run rally in the eighth inning — with the outcome long decided — to avoid being shut out entirely.

Milwaukee managed zeros in six of nine innings and was blanked through the first three frames before the dam burst in the fourth. Christian Yelich, pinch-hit for late in the contest, could do nothing to stop the bleeding for the Brewers. The Pirates, by contrast, spread their damage efficiently and cruised through nine innings in exactly three hours, collecting one of their most lopsided home wins of the 2026 season.

secondary.headline: YANKEES GRIND OUT LATE RALLY TO DOWN NATIONALS, 5-3
secondary.deck: New York plates two in the eighth and one in the ninth to escape Washington
secondary.body:
WASHINGTON — The New York Yankees refused to fold Sunday, rallying from a 3-2 deficit with two runs in the eighth inning and one more in the ninth to beat the Washington Nationals 5-3 before 33,699 at Nationals Park. Starter Cavalli earned the victory, and Alvarez also factored into the decision as New York's bullpen shut the door after the offense did its work.

Washington had led 3-2 entering the eighth after Jose Tena was hit by a pitch from Warren earlier in the game, and the Nationals held their one-run advantage into the late innings before New York's lineup broke through. The Yankees were held scoreless through the first four frames and needed five innings to plate their first run, but once they found their footing against the Washington staff they did not stop until they had turned a deficit into a comfortable two-run cushion.

secondary.headline: CUBS POUR IT ON IN SEVENTH, ROLL PAST REDS, 8-4
secondary.deck: Chicago scores four in the seventh inning to pull away after Cincinnati had led
secondary.body:
CINCINNATI — The Chicago Cubs fell behind early Sunday, watched Cincinnati score four times in the third inning, and then methodically dismantled the Reds the rest of the afternoon at Great American Ball Park, winning 8-4 before 29,200. A four-run seventh inning was the decisive blow, as Chicago totaled eight runs against a Cincinnati staff that included Boyd, who hit both Seiya Suzuki Stewart and Hayes with pitches during the game.

The Cubs scored twice in the first, went quiet while Cincinnati seized its 4-2 lead in the third, then added two more in the fourth to tie things at four before the seventh-inning explosion broke the game open. Alcantara, pinch-hit for in the seventh, could not prevent the Cubs from seizing control. Chicago recorded runs in four separate innings and blanked the Reds over the final six frames, securing a decisive road victory heading into the final stretch before the All-Star break.

secondary.headline: LEAFS FRONT OFFICE IN CHAOS AS WICKENHEISER SHOWN THE DOOR
secondary.deck: Toronto fires assistant GM Hayley Wickenheiser in sweeping front office purge
secondary.body:
TORONTO — One of hockey's most celebrated figures was pushed out Sunday as the Toronto Maple Leafs fired assistant general manager Hayley Wickenheiser as part of a sweeping purge of the front office. Wickenheiser, widely regarded as one of the greatest women's players in the history of the sport, had served in the Leafs' front office after transitioning from playing to management, but she was among several executives shown the door in what the organization signaled was a wholesale restructuring.

The firings sent shockwaves through the NHL community, arriving with the league's playoffs still ongoing and free agency already generating its own headlines. The Anaheim Ducks separately confirmed they will match the $90 million offer sheet tendered to young center Leo Carlsson, retaining the promising pivot at $18 million annually over five years. With rosters being shuffled across the league, Sunday proved to be one of the most turbulent non-game days in recent NHL memory.

column.headline: PITTSBURGH'S FOURTH INNING WASN'T BASEBALL — IT WAS AN EXECUTION
column.body:
Ten runs in one inning against a major league pitching staff is not a rally. It is a demolition. What the Pittsburgh Pirates did to the Milwaukee Brewers in the fourth inning Sunday at PNC Park went beyond timely hitting or good fortune — it was the kind of inning that breaks a team's spirit for a week. Milwaukee cycled through pitchers, and each one handed the baton to the next in worse shape than he received it. The Brewers did not lose a baseball game Sunday. They survived one.

The real question for Milwaukee after a 14-5 drubbing is how a club that looked helpless through three innings somehow failed to limit the bleeding once the Pirates found the gap. Three zeros against Pittsburgh's lineup early should have been a warning sign that the offense was going to need every run it could manufacture. Instead the Brewers gave up a crooked number of historic proportions and never recovered. Pittsburgh's lineup is dangerous when it gets going, and Sunday it got going all at once.

story.headline: RED SOX RALLY IN NINTH, WALK OFF IN TEN TO SINK METS AT FLUSHING
story.deck: Boston scores twice in the ninth to force extras, then wins it in the tenth.
story.body:
NEW YORK, July 12 — The Boston Red Sox looked finished at Citi Field, trailing the New York Mets 2-0 with three outs to go Sunday night. Then the ninth inning happened. Boston pushed across two runs to tie the game, and reliever Tolle earned his second win of the night when the Red Sox scratched out a run in the tenth to take a 3-2 decision before 37,638 fans, the largest crowd of Sunday's slate.

The Mets had held leads of 1-0 after the first and 2-1 after the sixth, and their bullpen held Boston scoreless through innings four, five, six, seven, and eight. Francisco Lindor contributed a home run, his fifth of the year, and a double for the home side, but New York's offense left 13 runners on base and could not add to its slim cushion. A pinch-hit double play by a batter hitting for Eaton in the ninth suggested the door was closing, but Boston refused to let it shut.

Elsewhere Sunday, Pittsburgh battered Milwaukee 14-5 at PNC Park in the day's highest-scoring affair, erupting for 10 runs in the fourth inning alone. Winning pitcher Yoho absorbed two hit-by-pitches issued to Bryan Reynolds but survived the rough stretch; home runs from Brent Turang, Marcell Ozuna, and Henry Davis paced the Brewers' offense in a losing cause. Baltimore also romped, 8-2 over Kansas City, with Salvador Basallo belting his 16th home run and the Orioles posting five runs in the sixth inning to blow a close game open.

story.headline: DYBANTSA DAZZLES IN POTENTIAL FINAL SUMMER AUDITION, LEADS WIZARDS TO VICTORY
story.deck: Top overall pick posts 23 points, seven rebounds in possible summer league finale for Washington.
story.body:
LAS VEGAS — AJ Dybantsa arrived at the Thomas & Mack Center with something to prove, and the No. 1 overall pick in the 2026 NBA Draft delivered emphatically Sunday, scorching the Sacramento Kings for 23 points and hauling in seven rebounds to lead the Washington Wizards to a summer league victory in what may have been his final showcase appearance of the offseason.

Dybantsa, the 18-year-old forward out of BYU who captivated the basketball world throughout the pre-draft process, showed precisely why Washington tabbed him atop the board. He attacked mismatches with a polished footwork arsenal that belied his age, converting mid-range pull-ups and finishing through contact at the rim. His seven rebounds underscored the two-way impact the Wizards are banking on as they attempt to rebuild around their prized cornerstone.

Whether Dybantsa suits up again this summer league remains uncertain, as the Wizards organization weighs the risk of additional minutes against the development benefits. Washington brass watched closely from the stands, and if Sunday's performance was indeed his curtain call in Las Vegas, Dybantsa left the desert with a statement ringing in everyone's ears heading into his first NBA training camp.

story.headline: DUCKS MATCH $90M OFFER SHEET, KEEP CARLSSON; LEAFS PURGE FRONT OFFICE IN WILD MONDAY
story.deck: Anaheim retains its 21-year-old star while Toronto shakes up management, firing Wickenheiser
story.body:
Anaheim matched Philadelphia's five-year, $90 million offer sheet for center Leo Carlsson on Monday, keeping the 21-year-old phenom in orange at a record $18 million per season — the richest offer sheet in NHL history. The Flyers had gambled that the Ducks, already navigating a tight salary cap picture, would balk at the price tag and surrender the young Swede. Anaheim blinked once, then held firm, writing the check and handing Carlsson a contract that will define the franchise for the next half decade.

Carlsson himself addressed the saga publicly Monday, calling the ordeal surreal but affirming his commitment to the Ducks' rebuild. The former second-overall pick has posted back-to-back strong seasons in Anaheim, emerging as one of the most dangerous two-way centers in the Western Conference. Philadelphia's aggressive bid signaled league-wide recognition of his elite ceiling, but Carlsson will remain the cornerstone of a young Ducks core that also includes Mason McTavish and Trevor Zegras.

Meanwhile in Toronto, the Maple Leafs turned their summer into a front-office earthquake, firing assistant general manager Hayley Wickenheiser as part of a sweeping management purge. Wickenheiser, a four-time Olympic gold medalist and one of the greatest women's players ever to lace up skates, had served in the Leafs organization since 2018. The dismissal signals a sharp change in organizational philosophy under ownership, with Toronto desperate to shake loose years of playoff disappointment and rebuild its decision-making structure from the top down.

story.headline: VETERANS SHUFFLED AS NFL ROSTERS TAKE SHAPE AHEAD OF SUMMER CAMPS
story.deck: Free agent signings and late trades continue to reshape the league's balance of power.
story.body:
The dust from April's draft has barely settled, and already the NFL's roster landscape looks dramatically different heading into the summer. The Dallas Cowboys made the boldest move of the post-draft period, agreeing to terms with veteran wide receiver DeAndre Hopkins on a one-year, $9 million deal, giving quarterback Dak Prescott a proven target as Dallas pushes back against a dominant NFC East. Meanwhile, the Jacksonville Jaguars shipped disgruntled offensive tackle Cam Robinson to the Las Vegas Raiders in exchange for a third-round pick in 2027, ending a long and public standoff between the lineman and the Jacksonville front office.

Around the league, the Pittsburgh Steelers continued their methodical rebuild under second-year coordinator Aaron Glenn, locking up linebacker Patrick Queen to a three-year extension worth $42 million. The move signals Pittsburgh's intent to anchor its defense before training camp opens in late July. The New England Patriots, still riding the energy of their first-round selection of Louisville quarterback Tyler Shough, added veteran backup Gardner Minshew on a modest one-year contract to provide insurance and mentorship during what the organization is openly calling a transitional year.

NFL analysts point to the defending Super Bowl LX champion Kansas City Chiefs as the benchmark every reshuffling roster is chasing. General managers across the league are under pressure to close the gap before September, and the coming weeks of minicamp and organized team activities will offer the first real measure of whether any challenger has done enough. Several coaches acknowledged this week that the window between now and the first preseason kickoff is shrinking fast.
